name: The Philosophical Zombie
statement: A being physically identical to you but with no inner experience at all seems at least conceivable, and that alone threatens the view that mind is nothing but matter.
statementAccent: seems at least conceivable, and that alone threatens
meaning: The philosophical zombie, or p-zombie, is a thought experiment in the philosophy of mind, used most influentially by the philosopher David Chalmers to argue against physicalism about consciousness. A philosophical zombie is a hypothetical being that is molecule-for-molecule identical to a normal conscious person and behaves exactly like one, yet has no conscious experience whatsoever: there is nothing it is like to be it, no inner feel to its states, the lights are off inside. It would say ouch when injured and claim to see colours, but experience nothing. The term itself was introduced by Robert Kirk in the 1970s. Chalmers argues that because such a being seems conceivable, without contradiction, consciousness cannot be simply identical to or wholly determined by the physical facts, since one could hold all the physical facts fixed while the experience varied or vanished. This is meant to establish the reality of the hard problem of consciousness.
mechanism: The zombie argument moves from conceivability toward metaphysical possibility and then to a conclusion about the nature of mind. First, a zombie, a physical duplicate lacking any consciousness, appears conceivable: we can coherently imagine it, finding no hidden contradiction. Second, Chalmers argues, what is ideally conceivable in this way is metaphysically possible: there could be a world physically just like ours but without consciousness. Third, if such a world is possible, then consciousness is not fixed by the physical facts alone, so physicalism, which holds that the physical facts settle everything, is false. The argument thus tries to show there is an explanatory gap between physical processes and subjective experience, the hard problem of consciousness. Its most contested step is the inference from conceivability to genuine possibility, and physicalists such as Daniel Dennett reject the argument, denying that zombies are truly conceivable and holding that the appearance of a gap is an illusion.

examples.text: A zombie flinches from fire, says that hurts, and reports seeing red just as you do, yet feels nothing at all; behaviour and physiology are identical, experience absent.
Chalmers argues that because a zombie world seems coherently conceivable, it is metaphysically possible, so consciousness is not fixed by the physical facts alone.
Daniel Dennett denies zombies are genuinely conceivable, holding that anything physically and functionally identical to a conscious being would in fact be conscious.

variants.name: The conceivability argument
variants.text: The general strategy of arguing from what can be coherently conceived, a zombie, to what is possible, and thence to a conclusion about the nature of mind.

variants.name: The hard problem of consciousness
variants.text: Chalmers's broader claim, which the zombie supports, that explaining why physical processes are accompanied by subjective experience is a distinct, hard problem.

whyItMatters: The philosophical zombie is one of the most debated thought experiments in the contemporary philosophy of mind, the centrepiece of Chalmers's case for the hard problem of consciousness and against physicalism. It sharpens the question of why any physical system should have subjective experience at all, dramatizing the apparent gap between objective physical description and the felt quality of inner life. The argument has driven a vast literature on conceivability, possibility, and the metaphysics of mind, forcing physicalists to explain either why zombies are inconceivable or why conceivability does not imply possibility. Whether or not one accepts its conclusion, the zombie has become a standard reference point for framing the mystery of consciousness and testing theories of how mind relates to matter.

working.text: conceive a being identical to a conscious person in every physical and behavioural respect but wholly lacking inner experience.
consider Chalmers's claim that if such a zombie is coherently conceivable, then it is metaphysically possible.
infer that if a physical duplicate could lack consciousness, then consciousness is not fixed by the physical facts, so physicalism is false, while noting the disputed steps.

limits: The zombie argument is contested at nearly every step, and its conclusion is a substantive philosophical position rather than settled fact. Critics, including Daniel Dennett, deny that zombies are genuinely conceivable, arguing that a full physical and functional duplicate of a conscious being would necessarily be conscious. Others accept that zombies are conceivable but deny that conceivability entails metaphysical possibility, breaking the crucial inference. Type-B physicalists hold that consciousness is physical even though the identity is not knowable a priori, which would let zombies be conceivable yet impossible. The experiment therefore frames a debate rather than resolving it, and its force depends on unresolved questions about the link between what we can imagine and what can really be.
misreadings: The philosophical zombie is not the shambling monster of horror films but a technical notion, a physical and behavioural duplicate lacking only inner experience. Conceiving a zombie is not by itself proof that physicalism is false; the argument needs the further, disputed claim that conceivability implies genuine possibility, which many reject. And the experiment does not show consciousness is non-physical as an established result; it advances a contested position, since physicalists deny either that zombies are truly conceivable or that their conceivability entails their possibility.
origin: The term philosophical zombie was introduced by Robert Kirk in the 1970s; the influential zombie argument against physicalism, moving from the conceivability of a non-conscious physical duplicate to the falsity of physicalism, was developed by David Chalmers, notably in his 1996 book The Conscious Mind.

sources.text: Philosophical zombie, Wikipedia. — the definition of a p-zombie as a non-conscious physical duplicate, Kirk's coinage of the term, Chalmers's conceivability argument against physicalism, and Dennett's rejection.
